bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Macro-economic environment and discretionary demand — Global economic uncertainty, inflationary pressures, elevated household indebtedness and fluctuations in consumer sentiment may impact discretionary spending; prolonged demand softness could affect sales growth, profitability and inventory productivity. Mitigation stated: presence across multiple consumer segments, categories and price points, disciplined cost management, agile planning, stronger inventory and working-capital management, sourcing flexibility and channel-mix optimisation. Structural concentration reinforcing this risk: exports are only 1.04% of total turnover and the sole international market named is the USA, so essentially all demand is Indian discretionary consumption (BRSR Section A, back-filled from the registry/governance bundles). The MD&A separately flags the West Asia conflict as the key near-term risk, through higher energy prices, freight costs and supply-chain disruptions.
- Adapting to evolving consumer behaviour — Rapidly changing consumer preferences, evolving lifestyles and increasing digital influence continue to reshape fashion consumption; failure to anticipate these shifts could impact product relevance, customer engagement and market share. Mitigation: continuous investment in consumer insights, product innovation, category expansion and digital capabilities, and a balanced portfolio across consumer segments and occasions.
- Information security and cyber resilience — Increasing use of digital platforms, interconnected systems and consumer data heightens exposure to cybersecurity threats, data breaches and operational disruptions; a significant incident could impact business continuity, stakeholder trust and brand reputation. Mitigation: cybersecurity and resilience framework with security controls, continuous monitoring, disaster recovery and business continuity, employee awareness programmes, vulnerability assessments and governance reviews; information and cyber security systems were independently assessed by one of the Big 4 audit firms.
- Retail expansion and occupancy costs — Increasing competition for premium retail locations may constrain access to high-quality spaces and result in higher occupancy costs, affecting expansion plans, store economics and profitability - directly material given 1,273 stores over 7.9 million sq ft and continued footprint addition. Mitigation: market presence and long-standing developer/landlord relationships, plus focus on store productivity, space utilisation and in-store experience to maximise returns.
- Talent attraction, retention and capability development — Scaling across multiple verticals - design, retail, marketing, e-commerce and more - increases the need for skilled talent in a competitive Indian fashion retail sector. Mitigation: leadership development, succession planning, capability building, employee engagement, a strong employee value proposition, internal mobility, and access to the Aditya Birla Group's consumer-segment talent pool.
- Competitive intensity — The Indian fashion and lifestyle market is highly competitive across organised and unorganised domestic players, international brands, digital-first businesses and emerging D2C brands; increased competition may lead to pricing pressure, higher customer acquisition costs and market-share erosion. Mitigation: brand equity, product innovation, wider consumer reach, differentiated cross-channel experiences, a diversified portfolio and omni-channel presence.
- Technology, digital and AI adoption — Reliance on digital platforms, automation, analytics and artificial intelligence brings risks of technology obsolescence, integration complexity, implementation challenges and evolving regulatory expectations; failure to adopt emerging technologies may impact operational efficiency and competitiveness. Mitigation: scalable platforms, phased implementation, strong governance, and continued investment in digital capability, data quality, process integration and responsible AI adoption.
- Execution and transformation risk — The growth strategy involves scaling multiple businesses, expanding the retail footprint, strengthening omni-channel capabilities, integrating new platforms and driving operational transformation; delays in execution, ineffective implementation of strategic initiatives or inability to realise expected benefits may impact growth, profitability and return on investment. TRUNCATION: the supplied MD&A text cuts off mid-sentence at 'Your Company m', so the mitigation paragraph for this risk - and any risk numbered 9 or beyond - is not available.

business.body:

- Ethnic described as a "scalable platform spanning well-known & marquee premium and designer led brands" and "India's largest & most comprehensive ethnic wear portfolio", with 2200 Cr+ annual revenue and 670+ stores across brands; it spans apparel, beauty, accessories and jewelry.
- Galeries Lafayette positioned as "setting new benchmarks in luxury retail with a differentiated, first-of-its-kind department store in India", with strong brand and celebrity collaborations driving footfalls.

business.body:
- [Ethnic — TCNS drag] The deck gives two readings of ethnic growth side by side: "Ethnic grew 4% vs LY" and "Ex. TCNS growth at 14%", indicating TCNS is materially diluting the reported ethnic number.

outlook.body:
- Shift strategic priority from portfolio creation and expansion towards profitable and sustainable growth, improving operating performance across brands currently in scale-up or turnaround phases.
- Convert the broad fashion portfolio into profitable scale - improving store productivity, strengthening unit economics, optimizing costs, managing inventory more efficiently, expanding margins and achieving defined profitability milestones across key brands.
- Move towards a more balanced growth model focused on revenue growth, operating discipline and long-term value creation as newer and turnaround businesses mature.
- Maintain a multi-vertical portfolio architecture that participates across price points, occasions, geographies and shopping behaviours - the largest ethnic wear portfolio, a leading luxury retail platform, a dominant masstige and value retail presence and one of the largest digital-first brand portfolios.
- Human capital strategy founded on 'World-Class Employee Experience driven by Data, Digital & Analytics', anchored on four pillars: strengthening the talent pipeline, elevating the ABFRL Culture Code, building a future-ready organisation for market leadership, and making ABFRL the destination of choice for top talent.
- Structured, technology-enabled recruitment using AI-driven tools and behavioural assessments; balanced lateral, leadership and early-career hiring; emphasis on digital, analytics, supply chain and design capabilities; diversity hiring and internal mobility.
- Build leadership succession depth via Talent Councils, a 9-box performance-potential framework, Emerging Councils (JB 6-9) and Leadership Councils (JB 4-5), and the STRIDE young-talent programme (BMTs, FMTs, CA Striders, B.Tech/M.Tech Striders).
- Scale capabilities across corporate, retail, warehouse, sampling units and manufacturing facilities as the Company expands across brands, formats and geographies, while driving productivity and cost optimisation.
- NOT DISCLOSED in the supplied text. The bundle section headed '=== DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY ===' does not contain a dividend distribution policy at all - it carries the Corporate Governance Report's sexual-harassment complaints table, a note on accounting treatment, and a list of 'Other Policies and Codes of the Company' with web links (CSR Policy, Related Party Transaction Policy, Policy for Determining Material Subsidiary Companies, Policy for determination of materiality of information or event, Policy for archival of documents, Policy on preservation of documents, Code of practices and procedures for fair disclosure - truncated). No dividend, payout, buyback, debt-reduction, credit-rating or reinvestment philosophy appears anywhere in the supplied governance text. The only adjacent statements are qualitative reinvestment intent in the Chairman's Message ('investing in technology, retail expansion and future growth platforms') and Form AOC-1's 'Proposed Dividend' row, which is a financial-statement annexure and is not reproduced.
- Sustainability 3.0 framework anchored on five strategic pillars - Sustainable Brands, Product Stewardship, Net Zero & Decarbonisation, Health Safety & Well-being, and Social Impact - with a vision for 2030 stated to be aligned with global climate goals; this follows Sustainability 1.0 (ReEarth - For Our Tomorrow, launched FY13) and Sustainability 2.0 (which had defined milestones for 2025).
- Product stewardship outcome: 95% of garments carried at least one sustainability attribute (BRSR Principle 2 states 95% of product have at least one sustainable attribute under the 'Sustainable Attributes' sustainable-sourcing methodology).
- Packaging: 99.8% of the packaging portfolio was sustainable; carton boxes are 100% cardboard made from recycled paper; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is applicable to the entity's activities and a waste collection plan is in place.
- Water: 22% of water recycled within facilities; the GRI index states ABFRL does not discharge to local water bodies (GRI 303-2 omitted as Not Applicable).
- Energy and climate: 550 KWp of rooftop solar capacity installed; Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG emissions, emissions intensity and reductions are reported in the Natural Capital chapter; climate governance is run through the Risk Management and Sustainability Committee (RMSC) with COSO + TCFD integration and IFRS S2 / TCFD alignment indexed.
- Occupational health and safety: zero fatalities during the year and 90,801 man hours of safety training; 100% of factories and warehouses assessed on health and safety practices and working conditions; zero high-consequence work-related injuries / ill-health / fatalities for both employees and workers in FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25.
- Human rights: 100% of plants and offices assessed for child labour, forced/involuntary labour, sexual harassment, discrimination at workplace and wages, and 100% assessed for workplace health & safety requirements; human-rights due diligence covers all tier-1 vendors, warehouses, retail stores, business offices and in-house factories; policy stated to be in line with UNGC Principles of Human Rights & Labor and Social Accountability 8000; child and forced labour prohibited across all vendor sites, enforced through regular vendor audits; POSH policy extends to third parties, clients and vendors.
- Governance and ethics: Anti-Fraud and Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy in place; NIL fines, penalties, punishments, compounding fees or settlements with regulators/law enforcement/judicial institutions for directors and KMP across Principles 1-9; nil disciplinary action for bribery/corruption and zero conflict-of-interest complaints in FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25.
- Independent third-party assurance and assessment: BRSR core carries Reasonable Assurance from the British Standards Institution; IMS audit by BVQI; facilities assessed on Higg Index FEM / FSLM by Bluwin; human rights assessment by KPMG; social impact assessment by Navgraam Development Consulting LLP; information and cyber security assessed by one of the Big 4 audit firms.
- STATED ABSENCE - R&D and capital expenditure in specific technologies to improve the environmental and social impacts of products and processes was 0 in both FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25, with the 'details of improvements' column reading 'NA'.
- STATED ABSENCE - ABFRL does not have a stated policy on Policy Advocacy (NGRBC Principle 7); it states it undertakes need-based advocacy through Aditya Birla Group memberships of the Retail Association of India and the Clothing Manufacturers Association of India. Principles 7 and 9 also carry '-' (no review frequency) in the NGRBC review table where P1-P6 and P8 are reviewed Quarterly / Half yearly.
- STATED ABSENCE / DISCLOSURE GAPS in the GRI index - GRI 302-2 (energy consumption outside the organization) omitted because information is unavailable/incomplete with the monitoring mechanism under progress; GRI 302-5 omitted as not applicable ('Our products do not consume direct energy'); GRI 403-10 (work-related ill health) omitted as not applicable on the stated basis that operations involve only cutting and stitching related work with no hazardous exposure. The two SASB chemical-management metrics carry '-' in the page-number column.
- STATED ABSENCE - no standalone Equal Opportunity Policy under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016; the Company relies on its Human Rights Policy instead. Grievance mechanisms exist for permanent workers (works committee, 20% male / 80% female composition) and permanent employees, but are stated as 'No' for other-than-permanent workers and other-than-permanent employees.
- Social and supply chain: sustainable sourcing procedure via the 'Sustainable Attributes' methodology; supplier environmental and social screening (GRI 308 / 414) and Higg FEM/FSLM coverage reported in Social and Relationship Capital; Life Cycle Assessments conducted; no vulnerable or marginalized group identified as a stakeholder group.
- Social Impact pillar covers education, health and sanitation, sustainable livelihoods, water stewardship, digitalisation and employee volunteering; CSR is applicable under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY26 expansion was retail-footprint led, not plant led. More than 180 new stores were added during the year, resulting in nearly 600,000 sq. ft. (nearly 0.6 million sq ft) of net retail space addition, with expansion momentum accelerating across priority markets; the Chairman's Message states the network now comprises 1,273 stores spanning over 7.9 million square feet, complemented by brand websites and leading digital marketplaces. New formats were launched - Galeries Lafayette (luxury) and OWND (value fashion, re-branded from Style Up); OWND alone added 34 stores while emphasis was also placed on optimizing its operating model, elevating merchandise architecture and building a scalable platform. TASVA strengthened its position in premium wedding wear through strategic expansion across key markets; Jaypore continued selective store expansion with stronger omni-channel capabilities; TCNS is in a transformation journey refreshing retail identity. E-commerce sales including TMRW grew more than 20% year-on-year to around 16% of revenue. The Company states it is investing in technology, retail expansion and future growth platforms. The fixed-asset footprint disclosed in BRSR Section A is 2 Factories, 3 Sampling Units and 6 Warehouses plus 7 named offices in India (row total printed as 18), with international plants and offices printed as a dash = stated NIL. STATED ABSENCE worth noting: BRSR Principle 2 Q1 reports R&D = 0 and Capex = 0 as a percentage of total R&D/capex invested in specific technologies to improve environmental and social impacts, for BOTH FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25, with the 'Details of improvements' column reading 'NA' (i.e. zero is stated, the explanation is unknown). outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- For consumer-facing sectors such as fashion retail the underlying environment remains constructive; demand may remain uneven in the near term but the medium-term consumption outlook remains structurally positive.
- Indian apparel retail market estimated at around Rs 10 lakh crore in FY2025-26, projected to exceed Rs 14 lakh crore by FY2029-30 at a 9% CAGR, driven by rising disposable incomes, urbanisation, deeper branded-apparel penetration and organised retail expanding into Tier-II and Tier-III cities.
- Organised retail currently accounts for approximately 41% of India's apparel market and is expected to outpace the overall category, supported by brand-led formats, stronger retail infrastructure, international brand entry, digital commerce and omnichannel capabilities.
- Global apparel market estimated at USD 1.84 trillion in calendar 2025, expected to reach around USD 1.9 trillion in 2026 (approximately 3.3% growth) and USD 2.54 trillion by 2033 at a 4.1% CAGR for 2026-2033; Asia Pacific was 40.8% of global apparel revenue in 2025.
- Category growth rates stated: the organised value fashion market is growing at more than 15%; the occasion wear (ethnic) segment is growing at over 11%; D2C fashion brands continue to outpace the broader e-commerce fashion market.
- Rising affluence - households in the Elite and Upper-Mid income cohorts growing 2X over 2019-30 versus less than 1X for lower cohorts (BCG X RAI 2022 chart), broadening the addressable market across premium, aspirational and value segments.
- Indian macro: real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% for FY2025-26 with the RBI's FY2026-27 projection of 6.6%; growth broad-based, led by private consumption and investment, supported by personal tax relief, GST-related changes and continued formalisation.
- Global macro: growth of around 3.4% in 2025, projected at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027 - continuity in the economic cycle rather than a sharp break, with inflation and geopolitical risk as watchpoints.
- Key near-term risk flagged: the West Asia conflict, through higher energy prices, freight costs and supply-chain disruptions, which could raise input costs and weigh on inflation and consumer sentiment.
- Structural sector shifts management expects to drive the business: transition from unorganized to branded retail (most pronounced in Tier-II/Tier-III cities), omni-channel integration, next-gen (Gen Z and millennial) fashion consumption, hyper-personalised customer engagement, faster fashion cycles and speed-to-market, quick commerce and faster fulfilment, sustainability/ESG as a differentiator, and data-led decision making and AI adoption.
- Recovery signals in India: early signs of recovery with consumers prioritising affordability, variety and price-value; festive and wedding-led demand, improving sentiment and traction in value and mass-premium formats have helped category momentum turn a corner.

The Company's strategic priority is expected to shift from portfolio creation and expansion towards profitable and sustainable growth, with focus on improving operating performance across brands that are in scale-up or turnaround phases.

Key priorities over the next few years are stated to include improving store productivity, strengthening unit economics, optimizing costs, managing inventory more efficiently, expanding margins and achieving defined profitability milestones across key brands.

Transition to Sustainability 3.0 with a vision for 2030 aligned to global climate goals, focused on Sustainable Brands, Product stewardship, Net-Zero & decarbonization, Health safety & well-being and Social Impact.

The AGM notice proposes re-appointment of Price Waterhouse & Co Chartered Accountants LLP as Statutory Auditors for a second term of 5 consecutive years, from the conclusion of the 19th AGM till the conclusion of the 24th AGM, at a remuneration of Rs 1.44 Crore plus tax for FY 2026-27. risks.note: Global economic uncertainty, inflationary pressures, elevated household indebtedness and fluctuations in consumer sentiment may impact discretionary spending; prolonged demand softness could affect sales growth, profitability and inventory productivity. Mitigation stated: presence across multiple consumer segments, categories and price points, disciplined cost management, agile planning, stronger inventory and working-capital management, sourcing flexibility and channel-mix optimisation. Structural concentration reinforcing this risk: exports are only 1.04% of total turnover and the sole international market named is the USA, so essentially all demand is Indian discretionary consumption (BRSR Section A, back-filled from the registry/governance bundles). The MD&A separately flags the West Asia conflict as the key near-term risk, through higher energy prices, freight costs and supply-chain disruptions.

Rapidly changing consumer preferences, evolving lifestyles and increasing digital influence continue to reshape fashion consumption; failure to anticipate these shifts could impact product relevance, customer engagement and market share. Mitigation: continuous investment in consumer insights, product innovation, category expansion and digital capabilities, and a balanced portfolio across consumer segments and occasions.

Increasing use of digital platforms, interconnected systems and consumer data heightens exposure to cybersecurity threats, data breaches and operational disruptions; a significant incident could impact business continuity, stakeholder trust and brand reputation. Mitigation: cybersecurity and resilience framework with security controls, continuous monitoring, disaster recovery and business continuity, employee awareness programmes, vulnerability assessments and governance reviews; information and cyber security systems were independently assessed by one of the Big 4 audit firms.

Increasing competition for premium retail locations may constrain access to high-quality spaces and result in higher occupancy costs, affecting expansion plans, store economics and profitability - directly material given 1,273 stores over 7.9 million sq ft and continued footprint addition. Mitigation: market presence and long-standing developer/landlord relationships, plus focus on store productivity, space utilisation and in-store experience to maximise returns.

Scaling across multiple verticals - design, retail, marketing, e-commerce and more - increases the need for skilled talent in a competitive Indian fashion retail sector. Mitigation: leadership development, succession planning, capability building, employee engagement, a strong employee value proposition, internal mobility, and access to the Aditya Birla Group's consumer-segment talent pool.
risks.risk: Talent attraction, retention and capability development

risks.note: The Indian fashion and lifestyle market is highly competitive across organised and unorganised domestic players, international brands, digital-first businesses and emerging D2C brands; increased competition may lead to pricing pressure, higher customer acquisition costs and market-share erosion. Mitigation: brand equity, product innovation, wider consumer reach, differentiated cross-channel experiences, a diversified portfolio and omni-channel presence.

Reliance on digital platforms, automation, analytics and artificial intelligence brings risks of technology obsolescence, integration complexity, implementation challenges and evolving regulatory expectations; failure to adopt emerging technologies may impact operational efficiency and competitiveness. Mitigation: scalable platforms, phased implementation, strong governance, and continued investment in digital capability, data quality, process integration and responsible AI adoption.

The growth strategy involves scaling multiple businesses, expanding the retail footprint, strengthening omni-channel capabilities, integrating new platforms and driving operational transformation; delays in execution, ineffective implementation of strategic initiatives or inability to realise expected benefits may impact growth, profitability and return on investment. TRUNCATION: the supplied MD&A text cuts off mid-sentence at 'Your Company m', so the mitigation paragraph for this risk - and any risk numbered 9 or beyond - is not available.
